title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells
summary: No final do século XIX, ninguém acredita que exista vida inteligente fora da Terra. Então um estranho cilindro cai do céu perto de Londres, e dele saem criaturas vindas de Marte com máquinas gigantes e armas terríveis. Um homem comum conta como tenta sobreviver e reencontrar a esposa enquanto a Inglaterra é tomada pelo medo e pela destruição.

chapters.title: The Falling Star
paragraphs: At the end of the nineteenth century, nobody believed that the Earth was being watched. People went about their small, busy lives, sure that they were the masters of the world. But across the dark gulf of space, minds that were greater than ours were looking at our planet with envious eyes. They were the Martians, and slowly and surely, they were making their plans against us.

I live in Woking, a quiet town in Surrey, south-west of London. I am a writer, and in those days I was writing about philosophy. I had a friend called Ogilvy, an astronomer, and one summer night he invited me to look at Mars through his telescope. I saw a small round planet, red and silent. While we were watching, Ogilvy saw a little flash of light on its surface.

“Look,” he said. “Something is happening there. A great explosion of gas.” For ten nights the flashes continued, and the newspapers wrote short reports about them. “Perhaps they are trying to send us a signal,” people joked. Nobody was worried. “The chances of anything coming from Mars are a million to one,” said Ogilvy.

Then, one night, many people saw a falling star. It came down in a line of green fire and landed on Horsell Common, a large open area of sand and grass near my house. Early in the morning, Ogilvy went to look for it, hoping to find a meteorite.

He found a huge hole in the sand. In the middle of the hole lay an enormous cylinder, about thirty metres wide. It was very hot, and it was covered with a thick, grey crust. Ogilvy walked around it, amazed. Then he heard a noise from inside. The top of the cylinder was turning, very slowly.

“It’s hollow!” he thought. “It’s made by someone! There are men inside, and they are trying to get out!” He ran to the town to get help. Soon everybody knew the news. By the afternoon, a crowd had gathered around the pit. People came from all the towns nearby, on foot, on bicycles and in carriages. Boys sold apples and ginger beer. It was like a holiday.

I went there too. I stood at the edge of the pit and looked down at the strange object. The top was still turning. Some of the people were laughing, and some looked nervous. “It must be men from Mars,” said a young man next to me. “I wonder what they look like.”

Suddenly the lid fell off with a loud ring of metal. Everybody went silent. Something began to come out of the dark hole. At first I saw only two large dark eyes. Then a grey, round body, as big as a bear, slowly appeared. It was wet and shiny, like leather. Long, thin arms like snakes moved around it. Its mouth had no lips, and it was shaking and dripping.

The crowd screamed and ran back. I was terrified, and yet I could not stop looking. The creature breathed heavily, as if the air of the Earth was too thick for it. It was clearly suffering in our heavier gravity. Then a second creature appeared behind the first. I turned and ran to the trees, and from there I watched the pit until the sun went down.

chapters.title: The Heat-Ray
paragraphs: As the evening came, the crowd slowly came back to the common. People are curious, and many of them were no longer afraid. A small group of men decided to go towards the pit with a white flag. Ogilvy was with them, and so was a man from the newspaper. They wanted to show the Martians that we were intelligent and friendly.

I was standing on a little hill, not far away. I saw the group walk slowly across the sand. Then I saw three flashes of green light come out of the pit, one after another. A strange humming sound began, and a long hump of something like a mirror rose slowly from the hole.

Then a beam of invisible heat touched the men with the flag. In a moment, every one of them burst into flames. They fell like burning trees. The beam moved across the common. The grass caught fire, the trees exploded, and a house in the distance began to burn. It all happened in total silence, except for the humming. I could not move. I was too shocked even to run.

The invisible ray passed close to me, and then it went away and the noise stopped. Darkness came down. Suddenly a great terror took hold of me, and I ran through the trees towards the town, crying like a child. I fell many times. When I reached the road, I saw people walking calmly near the station. They had heard nothing. One man was talking about the price of bread. “There’s been some trouble on the common,” he said. “They say it was the men from Mars.”

At home, my wife was waiting for me. I was white and dirty, and my hands were shaking. I told her everything. She was frightened, but I tried to comfort her. “They can hardly move,” I said. “The air is too heavy for them. They crawled out of the pit very slowly. Perhaps they can’t leave it at all. We will be safe here.”
That night I ate my dinner and drank some wine, and I began to feel brave again. I did not know it, but I was eating my last civilised dinner for many strange and terrible days.

The next morning, Saturday, everything seemed normal. The milkman came as usual, and the trains were running. But soldiers had arrived and surrounded the common. Guns were being brought from the army camp. I talked with my neighbour over the garden fence. “It’s a pity they’re so dangerous,” he said. “It would be interesting to know how they live. But I suppose the army will kill them today.”

In the afternoon, I heard the sound of guns from the common. Then the church tower near us fell down, and the roof of the college burst into flames. The Martians were using the Heat-Ray against the town. They were not trapped in the pit at all.

I ran to the inn and asked the landlord if I could borrow his horse and cart. “I need to take my wife to her cousins in Leatherhead,” I said. “It’s twelve miles away. I’ll pay you well, and I’ll bring it back tonight.”

He agreed. I quickly put a few things in the cart, helped my wife up, and drove away as fast as the horse could go. Behind us, black smoke was rising above Woking. As we went up the hill, I looked back. The houses near the common were burning, and the sound of the guns was getting louder.

chapters.title: The Fighting Machines
paragraphs: We arrived in Leatherhead at about nine o’clock that evening. My wife’s cousins welcomed us, and we had supper together. My wife was very quiet. When I said that I had to take the cart back to Woking, she held my hand. “Please don’t go,” she said. “Stay here with me.”

“I promised the landlord,” I said. “And I want to see what is happening. I’ll come back tomorrow.” I have often wished that I had listened to her. That was the last time I saw her face for a long time.

It was a dark, hot night, and a storm was coming. As I drove back towards Woking, I saw a green light fall from the sky. It was a third cylinder. Then the storm broke. Lightning flashed again and again, and the rain came down in a flood. In one flash of lightning, I saw something that made my blood go cold.

It was a monstrous machine, taller than a house, walking on three long metal legs. It was striding over the young trees and breaking them as it came. It had a body like a large metal pot, and long, swinging arms of steel. It moved quickly and easily, like a giant spider, and it made a terrible metallic noise. As it walked, it gave a great howl: “Aloo! Aloo!” Then a second machine appeared, coming straight towards me.

My horse was terrified. It turned too fast, and the cart fell over. I was thrown into the ditch, and the horse ran away into the dark. I lay in the water and watched the huge machines walk past. Under the second machine’s body, I saw something hanging, like a fisherman’s basket. Later I understood what it was for.

When they had gone, I crawled out of the ditch and walked through the rain. Near the road, I found the body of the landlord, the man who had lent me his cart. He was dead, with his neck broken. I felt sick and lonely. At last, wet and cold, I reached my own house. I locked the door, drank some whisky, and sat in the dark, shaking.

Later I went upstairs to the window of my study. Outside, Woking was burning. Many houses were destroyed, and the railway was on fire. Around the pit on the common, I could see three of the tall machines, moving in the red light.
At dawn, I saw a man in the garden. He was a soldier, an artilleryman, and his uniform was black with smoke. I called him in and gave him food. He told me his story.

“We had our guns ready on the common,” he said. “Then the Martians came out in those machines. They burned everything. My horse fell on me, and that saved my life. All the other men in my battery are dead. I hid under the horse until night.”
“Are the Martians in the machines?” I asked.
“Yes, inside the hoods, like men in a ship,” he said. “They are not just animals. They are the brains of those machines. Our guns can’t do anything against them.”

We decided to leave together. I wanted to go to Leatherhead, to my wife. He wanted to go to London to join his army again. We filled our pockets with food and some biscuits, and we walked out into the grey morning. All around us, the countryside was silent and empty. People had run away during the night, and dead bodies lay on the roads.

chapters.title: The Battle at the River
paragraphs: The artilleryman and I walked north towards Weybridge, where the River Wey joins the great River Thames. On the way, we passed soldiers who were setting up big guns behind the trees. Some of the people in the villages did not even understand the danger. An old man was trying to save his flower pots. “Don’t you know what’s coming?” shouted the artilleryman. “Death is coming!”

At Weybridge, there was a crowd of people near the river, all trying to get onto a small boat that was taking passengers across the water. They were carrying bags, boxes, birds in cages and even pieces of furniture. Everybody was pushing and shouting. I lost the artilleryman in the crowd.

Then we heard the sound of guns from far away. Everybody stopped and looked up. Above the trees, beyond the river, a Martian fighting machine appeared. Then another, and another, and another. Five of them were walking quickly across the fields towards us. They were so tall that they seemed to touch the clouds.

The people screamed and ran in all directions. Then the hidden guns near the village fired. A shell exploded right in the face of the nearest machine. Its hood burst open, and the Martian inside was blown to pieces. The headless machine did not stop. It walked on like a blind giant, crashed into the church tower, and fell into the river with a huge explosion of steam.

For a moment, I felt a wild hope. “They can be killed!” I thought. But the other Martians turned their Heat-Rays on the town. Houses exploded into flames, and the river began to boil. A great wave of hot water came towards me. I had jumped into the river to hide, and now I was nearly burned alive. I screamed with pain and pulled myself onto the muddy bank, half dead.
Through the steam, I saw the Martians collect the broken pieces of their dead companion. They carried him away carefully, and then they walked back across the fields. Somehow, they had not seen me.

I found an empty boat and floated down the river for many hours, too tired and hurt to row. The banks were burning, and smoke hid the sun. In the afternoon, near the village of Halliford, I climbed out and lay down in the grass. When I woke up, a man was sitting next to me. He was a curate, a young priest from the local church. His face was white, and his eyes were wild and empty.

“Why does God allow these things?” he said in a high voice. “What have we done? This morning I was walking in my garden, and then fire, earthquake, death! All our work, all our churches, destroyed. Is this the end of the world?”
“Be quiet,” I said. I did not like his crying. “You are a priest. You must be strong for other people. Religion should help you in times like this.”
“But what are these Martians?” he cried. “How can God allow them?”
“They are not invincible,” I said. “One of them was killed this morning. They are things that can die, like us.”

In the evening, we saw heavy black clouds moving slowly along the ground in the distance, near the river. Wherever the cloud went, nothing remained alive. The Martians had found a new weapon, a poisonous Black Smoke. The curate and I hid in an empty house, and then we began to walk towards London, away from the deadly smoke.

chapters.title: The Flight from London
paragraphs: Here I must leave my own story for a while and tell what happened to my younger brother. He was a medical student in London, and I learned all of this from him much later.

At first, London did not take the Martians seriously. On Saturday, the newspapers had a short report about the cylinder at Woking. On Sunday, my brother read that the Martians were moving, and he was worried about me. He went to Waterloo station to take a train to Woking, but the trains were not running. Nobody knew why. People were standing around, talking and laughing. They thought it was just a problem with the railway.

That night, the news became terrible. Men ran through the streets, banging on doors and shouting. “The Martians are coming! They’re using poison smoke! London is in danger!” My brother looked out of his window. All along the street, people were opening their windows and asking questions in their night clothes. Then the church bells began to ring. Far away, he heard the sound of heavy guns.

By Monday morning, the whole of London was running away. Millions of people filled the roads to the north and the east. There were carriages, carts, bicycles and thousands of people on foot. Rich men and poor men walked side by side. People fought for places on the trains. Some were trampled in the crowds. It was the beginning of the end of civilisation.

My brother took a bicycle from a shop and rode north. On a country road, he saw two men attacking two ladies in a small carriage. They were trying to steal their pony. My brother jumped off his bicycle and hit one of the men. The younger lady had a small gun, and she fired it at the other man. The thieves ran away.

The ladies were Mrs Elphinstone, a doctor’s wife, and her young sister-in-law. Mrs Elphinstone was frightened and kept asking for her husband. The younger woman, Miss Elphinstone, was brave and calm. “Will you come with us?” she asked my brother. “We are going to the coast. We hope to find a ship to France.”

My brother agreed. For two days they travelled east together, through crowds of desperate people. They slept in the fields and shared their little food. At last they reached the sea at the mouth of the River Blackwater. Hundreds of ships of every kind were waiting there, full of refugees. My brother paid a lot of money for places on a small steamer that was going to Ostend.

As the steamer was leaving, three Martian fighting machines came walking through the shallow water towards the ships. The passengers screamed. Then a long, low warship came at full speed between the Martians and the boats. It was the Thunder Child, a torpedo ram of the Royal Navy.

The Thunder Child did not fire. It rushed straight at the nearest Martian. The Heat-Ray hit it, but the ship kept going, burning, and crashed into the giant machine. The Martian fell into the sea. Then the Thunder Child fired its guns and hit a second Martian. A moment later, the ship exploded in a cloud of fire and steam.

When the smoke cleared, the little steamer was far away. My brother and the two ladies looked back. The sun was going down, and over the land behind them, something flat and grey was flying through the sky. It was a Martian flying machine. They watched in silence as the coast of England disappeared into the evening.

chapters.title: Trapped in the Ruined House
paragraphs: Now I return to my own adventures. The curate and I hid for a day in an empty house while the Black Smoke moved around us. When it was gone, we walked through a grey, silent world. Everything was covered in black dust, and dead people lay in the streets. We were hungry and tired, and we moved slowly towards the south-west of London, hoping to find a way round the Martians to Leatherhead.

In the village of Sheen, we found a house with some food in the kitchen: bread, tins of meat, and bottles of water and wine. We were eating when suddenly there was a blinding green light and a terrible crash. The whole world shook. The ceiling fell on us, and I was knocked unconscious.
When I woke up, it was dark. The curate was holding my arm. “Don’t move,” he whispered. “Something is outside.” After a while, we heard strange metallic sounds and a low humming, very close to us.

When daylight came through a crack in the wall, I looked out. I could hardly believe my eyes. A fifth cylinder had fallen right next to the house. Half the house was destroyed, and we were in the kitchen, at the edge of an enormous pit. Down in the pit, the Martians were working. We were trapped.

For the first time, I could watch the Martians closely. They were the strangest creatures I have ever seen. Each one was really just a huge round head, about a metre and a half wide, with two large eyes and a sort of beak. Around the mouth there were sixteen thin tentacles, like hands. They had no stomachs and did not eat. Instead, they took the fresh, living blood of other creatures and put it straight into their own veins. I will not describe this in detail, because it is too horrible.

They had brought with them some other creatures from Mars: tall, weak animals with two legs, which they used as food. And they had also brought machines of every kind. One of them was a busy, crab-like thing with five legs and many arms, which dug the earth and made bars of shiny aluminium. It moved so naturally that at first I thought it was alive.

The curate and I lived in that dark kitchen for many days. We hardly dared to breathe. We took turns looking through the crack in the wall, and we argued in whispers about who could look. The curate ate and drank much more than his share. He cried, he prayed loudly, and he did not listen to me. I began to hate him.
“Be quiet!” I whispered. “If they hear us, they will kill us both.”
“I have been silent too long,” he said. “God wants me to speak. I must tell everybody what I have seen.”

One evening, I saw a terrible thing through the crack. The Martians brought a man to the pit. He was well dressed and fat, and he was fighting. A long metal arm lifted him up, and then I turned away. I could not look. But I heard his screams, and I understood what the Martians did with people. I understood what the basket under the fighting machine was for. We were their food.

chapters.title: The Days of Silence
paragraphs: After that night, the curate became worse and worse. On the eighth day, he stopped whispering and began to speak out loud. I had hidden the food and water in the pantry, but he wanted it all. “I have been praying for days,” he said. “Now I must give my message. I must go out and tell the people. Woe to this unfaithful world!”
He stood up and walked towards the broken door. His voice became louder and louder. “Woe! Woe! The voice of the Lord!”

I was terrified. If the Martians heard him, they would find me too. I picked up a heavy meat chopper from the kitchen table and hit him on the back of the head with the handle. He fell to the floor and did not move. I stood over him, breathing hard.

Then I heard a sound outside. Something was moving against the wall. Slowly, a long metal arm came through the hole in the wall, with many joints, like a snake. It moved around the room, touching things. I ran into the coal cellar and hid in the dark among the coal and wood. I heard the arm find the curate’s body and drag it out through the hole. I never saw him again.

Then the arm came back. It came into the coal cellar. It touched the coal. It touched the heel of my boot. I nearly screamed. Then it went away, holding a piece of coal. For a long time I lay there without moving, praying that it would not come back.

For the next few days, I was alone in the dark. The Martians had taken the water from the pantry, and I was terribly thirsty. I drank a little dirty rainwater from a pump in the kitchen. I hardly slept. I lost all sense of time.

During those days, a strange red plant began to grow everywhere. The Martians had brought its seeds from their own planet. It grew very fast, especially near water. Soon it covered the walls of the house and filled the crack in the wall like a red curtain. Through it, the light became red, and I felt as if I were living inside a strange, bloody cave.

On the fifteenth day, I noticed that everything was silent. I could hear no humming, no machines, no Martian sounds at all. A dog came and sniffed at the hole in the wall, and then I heard birds. For a long time I did not dare to move. At last I crawled to the hole and looked out.

The pit was empty. The Martians had gone. Their machines had gone too, except for a few broken pieces lying in the sand. Black birds were walking around in the bottom of the pit, eating something. I climbed out of the ruins of the house and stood in the sunlight.

I was alone, and I felt like the last man on Earth. The whole village had disappeared. Where there had been houses and gardens, there were now only hills of broken bricks, covered with the red weed. The sky was blue, and the air was warm, but there was no one anywhere. I was free, but I was in a dead world. I was weak with hunger, and I did not know where my wife was, or whether she was alive.

chapters.title: The Man on Putney Hill
paragraphs: I walked slowly through the empty country. In a garden I found some young onions and carrots, and I ate them raw. The red weed was everywhere, along the rivers and in the fields. I decided to walk towards Leatherhead, but I also wanted to know what had happened to London.

On Putney Hill, I saw a man with a sword in his hand, standing in a garden. He looked dirty and dangerous. “Stop,” he shouted. “Where do you come from? This is my place. There isn’t enough food for two.” Then he looked at me more carefully. “Wait. Aren’t you the man from Woking?”
It was the artilleryman! We shook hands, and he took me into the house where he was living. He gave me some food and a little wine, and we talked for hours.

“It’s all over,” he said calmly. “We’re beaten. They have conquered us, just as men conquer ants. Their flying machines have gone north. More cylinders are coming every day. London is empty. Most people have run away or died.”
“Then what can we do?” I asked.

His eyes became bright. “I’ve been thinking,” he said. “The Martians won’t kill all of us. They’ll keep some people, like cattle. Most people will be happy in cages, I’m sure. They will be fed and kept fat, and they won’t have to work. But not me. I’m going to live underground.”

He explained his great plan. “There are the drains and the sewers under London. Hundreds of miles of them. We’ll live there. We’ll collect strong, clever men and women, and we’ll take books and learn science. We won’t let weak or stupid people join us. Then one day, we’ll capture a fighting machine and learn how to use it. And then, ha! We’ll turn the Heat-Ray against them! We’ll make them run!”

For a while I believed him. His words gave me hope. He showed me a tunnel which he had already started to dig from the cellar of the house towards a big sewer. I helped him dig all morning. But after a few hours, I looked at the tunnel and did some sums in my head. He had dug only about ten metres in a whole week. At this speed, he would need many years to reach the sewer.

In the afternoon, he stopped working. “Let’s go up on the roof and look around,” he said. Then he wanted to eat, then to drink some champagne he had found, and then to play cards. We played cards all evening, and he laughed and talked about his great future. I began to understand him. He was a dreamer. He had big plans, but he was lazy. He would never do any of these things.

That night, I went up on the roof alone. I looked towards London. There was a strange green light in the sky to the north. Everything was quiet. I thought of my wife, and I felt ashamed. Here I was, playing cards and drinking wine, while the world was dying.

“I can’t stay here,” I said to myself. Early the next morning, while the artilleryman was still asleep, I left the house. I did not say goodbye. I wanted to go into London to see what the Martians were doing, even if it meant death.

chapters.title: Dead London
paragraphs: I crossed the river and walked into London. It was the strangest thing I have ever seen. The great city, where millions of people had lived, was completely empty. Shops were open, but nobody was inside. Carts stood in the streets with no horses. Black dust covered everything, and here and there I saw dead bodies. The silence was terrible.

Then, as I came near Hyde Park, I heard a sound. It was a howl, very sad and very long: “Ulla, ulla, ulla, ulla.” It went on and on, without stopping. It seemed to fill the whole city. I walked towards it, half afraid and half curious.

Near Regent’s Park, I saw a Martian fighting machine standing very still above the trees. The howling came from it. I waited, but it did not move. Then, suddenly, the sound stopped. The silence after it was even more frightening than the noise.

I was so tired and so lonely that I no longer cared about my life. “Let them kill me,” I thought. “I want to end this.” I walked straight towards the Martians’ largest pit, on Primrose Hill. The sun was rising. I climbed to the top of the hill and looked down.

The pit was enormous, and it was full of machines. Some were standing, some had fallen over. And everywhere, lying on the ground, were the Martians. They were not moving. Black birds were pulling at their bodies. Dogs were eating them. The Martians were dead. All of them were dead.

At first I could not understand. Then, slowly, the truth came to me. The Martians had not been killed by our guns or our ships. They had been killed by the smallest creatures in the world: bacteria. On Mars there were no diseases, and the Martians had no protection against our germs. From the moment they arrived, the tiny bacteria in our air and water had been killing them. Our human bodies have fought these germs for millions of years, and we have learned to live with them. The Martians could not.

I stood on the hill and cried. I raised my hands to the sky and thanked God. The great city around me was not dead after all. It would live again. Then I lost my senses, and for three days I knew nothing. Some kind people found me wandering in the streets, talking to myself, and they took care of me.

When I was well again, the news had spread all over the world. Food was arriving from France and other countries. Trains and ships were bringing people back to London. Everybody was weeping and laughing at the same time. But I had one thought only. I went back to Woking to find my wife.

My house was still standing. The door was open, and inside everything was as I had left it on that first terrible night. On my desk was the page I had been writing about philosophy. I was sure my wife was dead. I stood in the empty room, and I felt that it was all hopeless.

Then I heard a voice outside the window. “It’s no use,” somebody said. “The house is empty.” I turned round. There, on the path, stood my wife’s cousin, and next to him, white and trembling, was my wife.
“I came,” she said. “I knew... I knew...” She put her hand to her throat and began to fall. I ran out and caught her in my arms.

Even now, years later, I sometimes wake in the night and see the black smoke and the tall machines. And I wonder if the Martians will come again. We have learned that our planet is not safe, and that we are not the masters of the universe. But when I look at the people in the busy streets of London, alive and laughing, I am thankful for every one of them.
